newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China injects openness into Hong Kong leadership race.
newsitem.headline: China injects openness into Hong Kong leadership race.

text.p: Beijing signalled on Friday it was trying to choose Hong Kong's future leader in a transparent way, drawing a cautious welcome in the nervous British colony in the run up to its handover to China next year.

Hong Kong government radio reported that a set of rules worked out by a panel in Beijing on Thursday would make it possible for the public to see who was backing whom in the process of choosing Hong Kong's post-colonial chief executive.

"The procedures for selection of the chief executive proposed in Beijing...provide a welcome recognition of the importance of transparency in picking the person who will guide Hong Kong's future," the South China Morning Post said.
"After months of speculation, it appears a more open-minded attitude has prevailed than many in the territory had expected," the English-language daily said in an editorial.

The chief executive who will take over from Governor Chris Patten on July 1, 1997, will be chosen by a 400-member Selection Committee, itself to be named soon by Beijing's Preparatory Committee overseeing the handover -- that much was known.
But many had feared the committee would just rubber-stamp a candidate pre-approved by Beijing, without much debate on who the candidate was or what he or she stood for.

On Thursday, a panel of the Preparatory Committee proposed each candidate should be nominated by at least 50 members of the Selection Committee, and that the names of the nominators should be published, government radio reported.
That allows for scrutiny by the Hong Kong public and press of exactly who is backing each candidate.

The number on nominators was also cut from 100 considered earlier, raising the number of possible candidates to eight, and allowing more committee members to avoid having to pledge their support too early in the process.
The candidates will have to present themselves to the Selection Committee in front of the media, reports from Beijing said.
"The accounts they provide of their intentions -- and perhaps a full electoral platform -- will thus be passed on to the public through the press, radio and television," the Post said.
The 400 members of the committee would then vote by secret ballot, with support of at least half required for election.
"Any candidate who wants to be elected must win the trust of (all sectors) of the Selection Committee and win the support of the majority," Beijing's Hong Kong mouthpiece, the daily Wen Wei Po said.
"This type of democratic election is the realisisation of Hong Kong's people's participation and will produce a chief executive who will command public respect and support," it said.
The proposals have to be approved by the full Preparatory Committee next month, but no major changes are expected.
Not everyone was convinced by Beijing's softer tone, noting it still plans to replace the elected legislature (Legco) with an appointed council and repeal local laws it does not like.
"I think there may be a bit of an effort to make it look less secretive, it's like the general Chinese charm offensive of the last couple of weeks," said China watcher Jonathan Mirsky.

"We know what China will do when it gets here, it will get rid of Legco, it will have its own chief executive, its own garrison, it'll get rid of the Bill of Rights, it'll move the court up to Peking," he said.
